Home Posts Signal #73: $6 Billion, No Acquisition Signal #73: $6 Billion, No Acquisition NVIDIA paid six billion dollars for a software pipeline and 109 engineers without buying the company that owned them. Ukraine, Britain and Hugging Face are all working the same seam this week. Çelik Nimani Aug 26, 2026 • 5 min read In partnership with NVIDIA spent six billion dollars this week and did not buy a company. It licensed the software pipeline, hired the 109 people who built it, and left the corporate shell standing with its founders still inside. That structure shows up four times in this issue, across four industries. Ukraine handed its ground-robot design to a Finnish manufacturer instead of selling the company that made it, Britain got into the sensor archive Ukraine built through a treaty rather than a contract, and the one asset nobody has worked out how to unbundle is quietly looking for a buyer at thirteen billion. NVIDIA paid $6 billion and left the company standing On 21 August NVIDIA told investors it will pay Poolside $6 billion to license Model Factory , the pipeline Poolside used to build its Laguna coding model, and hire 109 engineers who built it. It is separately putting $1 billion into the company at a $12 billion pre-money valuation. The three founders stay. Poolside says it will pass the $6 billion through to its investors by the end of 2027. No acquisition, no change of control, nothing for a competition regulator to review. NVIDIA has now run this play three times: roughly $20 billion with Groq, about $900 million with Enfabrica, and now Poolside. What it buys is a capability and the people who carry it, priced as a software licence. What it avoids is the shell, the liabilities, the filing, and the awkwardness of owning a competitor to the labs it sells chips to. None of it lands in an M&A league table, which is why the totals in your favourite deal tracker have started to look small against what is happening. For a European deep-tech team, this is the exit conversation to prepare for. Not "what is the company worth" but "what does the pipeline license for, and how many of your people come with it." That changes what you protect in diligence, what sits in your employment contracts, and who at the table gets paid. A founder optimising for a clean acquisition is rehearsing a deal shape the largest acquirer in the industry has stopped using. Everything GTM. One platform. Small teams don't have time to stitch together five tools and hope it works. Apollo gives you everything you need to find leads, reach them, and close deals — all in one place: 230M+ verified contacts AI-powered outreach Data enrichment Inbound lead capture Meeting scheduler And more Stop juggling tools and start building pipeline that scales. With Apollo, the AI revenue engine powering 4M+ users. Sign up for free Ukraine gave Finland the blueprint and kept the output On 23 August, in front of Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Alexander Stubb, Ukraine and Finland signed three documents : drone development and production on Finnish soil, maritime unmanned systems, and a facility for unmanned ground robots. Seven Finnish companies are named, among them Patria, Nokia, ICEYE, Sensofusion and Insta. Under that umbrella Ukraine's Tencore and Finland's Insta turned a February memorandum into a joint venture that will build TERMIT 2.0 ground vehicles in Finland, with an initial target of 320 systems for Ukraine's forces. Stubb has put the output split at 90/10 in Ukraine's favour. Tencore did not sell. It licensed a design proven under fire into a NATO industrial base, and the build runs across a spread of Finnish partners rather than one plant. Ukraine gets units it cannot safely produce at home at that volume. Finland gets a product line, a supply chain, and four years of combat iteration it could never have generated on its own. The design stays Ukrainian, and so does Tencore. Watch the phrase "distributed model involving industrial partners," because that is the opening. A ground-robot programme spread across Finnish subcontractors needs drives, optics, power electronics, comms and enclosures, and almost none of that is locked down yet. If you make components anywhere between Tallinn and Kraków, the qualification window on this line is open now and closes once the first 320 units are specified. Hugging Face is for sale because nobody can license it Business Insider reported on 24 August that Hugging Face has hired a bank and is weighing bids at around $13 billion . Its last priced round was $4.5 billion in 2023, led by Salesforce Ventures with Alphabet, GV and IBM Ventures. Earlier this year it turned down $500 million from NVIDIA at a $7 billion valuation, on the grounds that a single investor would carry too much influence. No buyer is named, nothing is signed, and the company has not commented. Treat the number as an ask, not a price. The contrast with Poolside is the whole story. Hugging Face's value is not a pipeline you can copy or a team you can hire away. It is a registry, a community and a default that millions of workflows already point at, and none of that detaches from the company that runs it. Assets built that way still have to be sold whole. Everything else is being unbundled around them. Same week, different shape: Stability AI raised $76 million from Universal Music, Sony Music, Warner Music, Electronic Arts and AMD Ventures, taking it to $232 million raised in total. Almost every name on that list is also a licensing counterparty. They took equity instead of, or alongside, a cheque for rights. Any studio, catalogue owner or data holder in this region sitting across from a model vendor should read that structure closely, because the term sheet is the licence now. Britain bought Ukraine's battlefield data with a treaty On 24 August the UK and Ukraine signed a military AI partnership in Kyiv that gives Britain access to Avengers AI Labs, Ukraine's targeting and analysis platform. Avengers ingests feeds from thousands of daylight cameras and infrared sensors and has produced millions of labelled object identifications: tanks, artillery, air defence, infantry, drones, reconnaissance UAVs. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and AI Minister Kanishka Narayan signed alongside Zelenskyy, setting up a joint AI cell of engineers, academics, companies and serving military. No value was disclosed, because there is no purchase price. The scarcest input in defence AI did not move through a commercial licence. It moved through a bilateral state agreement, which means the route to it runs through your own government rather than a sales conversation. Three British startups took the first pilots: Sintela in Bristol on fibre-optic sensing for base protection, Mind Foundry in Oxford, and Skyral in London. In the same package MBDA was cleared to release classified information about UK components of the SCALP missile so assembly can happen inside Ukraine. Poland, Romania, the Baltics and Czechia all have edge-AI and sensing companies that would be remade by that dataset, and every one of them is waiting on a ministry rather than a purchase order. Ask whoever runs defence-industrial policy in your capital what their agreement with Kyiv says about data. If the answer is that there isn't one, you are looking at the exact distance between a national AI strategy and a defence-tech sector. Short Signals Five things to install or check this week, tagged by the seat they help. Productivity: OpenAI put admin controls inside the chat. The Admin plugin shipped on 25 August for ChatGPT Work and Codex, letting admins query usage, manage members and groups, gate model access by role and approve limit requests without leaving the conversation. OpenAI says its own IT team now resolves around 45% of ticket volume this way. If you run a team on ChatGPT Work, this kills the console round-trip that turned an access request into a day. Design: Alibaba's Wan 3.0 takes a PDF as input. Released on 24 August , it generates 30-second clips with audio from text, image, video or audio references, and accepts DOC, XLS, PPT, PDF and Markdown as source material. A 30% API discount runs to 23 September, and it is already live on Vercel's AI Gateway. Point it at a product one-pager before you brief an agency to make the same thing. Dev: Vercel Connect ends the stored API key. Generally available on 25 August , it issues short-lived scoped tokens to agents at runtime across more than 100 preset connectors including Notion, Slack, GitHub, Snowflake and Workday, plus generic OAuth and MCP servers. Hobby covers 500 token requests a month free, Pro runs $3 per 1,000. Worth an hour if any agent you run currently reads a credential out of an environment variable. Research: DeepSeek priced vision like text. V4-Flash-Vision-Exp landed on 21 August , matching V4-Flash on text while pushing multimodal agent scores toward the frontier. Images bill at up to 384 tokens each at flash rates, and the Files API is free with image reuse by file ID. Document-reading agents have been the expensive half of every back-office automation pitch in this region. Run your ugliest invoice and contract samples through it before you quote a client. Founders: Romania's €1bn tech scheme is law, and your county sets the cheque. HG 643/2026 was published on 24 August : RON 5.31bn split between regional investment aid and R&D, projects of RON 5m to 50m, up to 30% advance on the R&D leg and a 200% tax deduction on eligible spend. Aid intensity runs from 30% in Timiș to 70% in Galați, Dolj and Gorj. Bucharest is excluded outright. Site selection now moves the grant more than the product does. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/27/how-.text: Russia has long regarded Belarus as a convenient reserve for topping up its manpower in the war against Ukraine, especially after suffering heavy losses at the front.Minsk’s economic dependence, the political vulnerability of Aliaksandr Lukashenka's regime and the legal uncertainty around the Union State create conditions in which the Kremlin can act with considerable freedom.In the Belarusian corner of the internet, in recent months a large number of adverts offering Belarusians the chance to sign a contract with the Russian army, have appeared. They are circulated everywhere – in Telegram channels, in Viber chats and in local community pages where people discuss everyday issues.At times it looks almost surreal: nestled between posts about selling vegetables or finding a tutor, a sudden offer appears promising a "high salary, benefits and Russian citizenship" in return for going to war.Investigations by DW, TVNET, CityDog and Current Time have documented a sharp increase in such posts. The human rights initiative Belpol regularly highlights examples of adverts in which recruiters use Belarusian phone numbers to inspire trust.On Belpol’s Telegram channel you can see messages promising huge payouts, help with loans, "annulment of criminal convictions" and fast-track Russian citizenship.On X, the OSB Belpol account posts screenshots of ads in which Belarusians are offered a contract with a one-off payment of 4.35 million roubles and rapid issuance of a Russian passport.These examples are not isolated incidents but part of a systematic campaign targeting socially vulnerable people.What recruiters promiseBelarusians are promised the equivalent of tens of thousands of euros, high salaries, housing, food, a military pension and life insurance.Some adverts even talk about "sorting out problems with the law," which is particularly dangerous given that participation in an armed conflict abroad falls under the article on mercenary activities in Belarus' criminal code which carries a prison term of up to seven years.Recruiters insist that the service is "legal," claiming it is not mercenary activity but "service in the army of the Union State."Who signs up for a contract?Research shows that among those recruited, the majority are men from small towns and villages, people on low incomes, with debts or with existing legal problems.Many do not realise the legal consequences and some are simply looking for quick money, without understanding that they will be sent to the most dangerous sectors of the front.Human rights activists point out that foreign contract soldiers are often placed in assault units, where casualty rates are particularly high.The recruitment scheme is simple and effective. A person sees an advert on social media and writes to the recruiter, who is using a Belarusian phone number. They are then told about payments, benefits and the supposed "legality" of the service.After that they are offered rapid paperwork and travel to Russia – most often via Smolensk or Pskov. There they sign a contract and become a member of the Russian armed forces. At that point there is almost no way back.For those who agree to sign a contract, the consequences can be tragic. Beyond the risk of being killed, they face criminal liability in Belarus, possible loss of citizenship or restrictions on their rights.Many end up as "cannon fodder" in someone else’s war, which they often barely understand.Public and state responseBelarusian society has generally reacted to this with alarm.People complain about mass spam-recruitment; some turn to the Interior Ministry, but there is virtually no response.The Lukashenka regime does not officially acknowledge that recruitment is taking place, but it does nothing to stop it.Belarus is far too dependent on Russian subsidies to openly confront the Kremlin.Furthermore, mobilisation measures inside the country are being stepped up, adding extra pressure on men of conscription age.Recruitment as part of Kremlin strategyThe recruitment of Belarusians is not about random adverts or the haphazard initiative of individual actors. It is a coordinated campaign built into the Kremlin’s strategy for expanding its pool of manpower for the war against Ukraine.The legal framework of the Union State gives Moscow extra room for manoeuvre: formally, citizens of Belarus and Russia have "equal rights" and Russian institutions are trying to spin this as "equal obligations," including compulsory military service.The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) warns that such an interpretation could become a basis for exerting pressure on Belarusians and attempts to mobilise them.Russia is exploiting the vulnerability of Belarusian society, its information isolation and Minsk’s political dependence in order to turn Belarus into a source of manpower.And the longer the war drags on, the more aggressive this campaign becomes.

Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters View image in fullscreen House prices in Australia are at the same point they were a year ago, the latest Cotality data shows. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters Housing Brisbane and Sydney hit hardest by falling house prices as 5.2% shaved from Australian property values Cotality data shows median house prices fell in September as interest rates hit borrowing capacity Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Luca Ittimani Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Housing prices are falling in almost every suburb in Australia’s biggest cities, with values dropping faster in Brisbane than Sydney as the slowdown intensifies. Prices nationally have fallen 5.2% from their peak in March to where they were a year ago, Cotality data released on Thursday shows. Economists say prices are on track to fall at least 10% after the Reserve Bank lifted rates for the fourth time this year on Tuesday, pushing more buyers out of the market. Brisbane’s home prices dropped 1.5% in September, with every suburb in the city recording lower prices compared with June. The median Brisbane home was worth $1.05m, down by $59,000 since May. The Queensland capital had seen prices surge 18% over the preceding 12 months. Sydney median values dropped 1.4% in the month and were down 8.6% from their record high in March, the equivalent of a $112,000 drop. Just four Sydney suburbs held steady in recent months. Suburb table Melbourne prices were down 7.2%, or $63,000, from November 2025. While a handful of suburbs have seen prices continue to rise, Joe Trucchio, a buyer’s agent at Property Home Base, said the downturn had swept the city. “We’re fully into the spring buying carnival, and we haven’t seen it pick up the way that it had in previous years,” Trucchio said. “It just takes some time and it takes some good news and right now we’ve had a sequence of bad news.” Interest rates have become “the biggest conversation” among hesitant buyers, Trucchio said. Comparison website Canstar has estimated this year’s four hikes have cut $47,400 from the borrowing capacity of someone earning an average annual full-time wage of $108,650. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Housing prices would have to fall roughly 10% to offset a 1 percentage point increase in interest rates and no suburbs have reached that threshold. However, Trucchio said dwellings on the cheaper end of the market had garnered more interest as first home buyers regained confidence. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The Albanese government on Thursday reported over 102,000 people had been supported with first home loans under the 5% deposit scheme in the year since it was expanded. The scheme has supported over 8,400 new first home buyers a month since June on average, relatively stable compared to the 8,600 a month average from October to May. The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, said on Tuesday the central bank considered leaving rates on hold amid an unexpectedly weak housing market but ultimately decided to lift. She said falling prices would probably worsen housing supply by making new construction unprofitable. Economists expect Australia’s shortage of housing will force home prices back up in future, though the receding chance of interest rates cuts has made a longer downturn more likely. AMP chief economist, Shane Oliver, said the Cotality data supported forecasts of prices falling at least 10% nationally. “Rate hikes, tax hikes and poor confidence are the big drags but rising distressed listings with rate hikes and rising unemployment do risk a deeper fall of around 15%,’” Oliver said. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: US secretary of State, Marco Rubio, center, and US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, arrive to board a plane near Athens, on his way to Portugal, on 8 October. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen US secretary of State, Marco Rubio, center, and US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, arrive to board a plane near Athens, on his way to Portugal, on 8 October. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AFP/Getty Images Trump administration Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports of improper conduct Senior official says president and US secretary of state are ‘extremely pissed off’ by conduct of US envoy to Greece Associated Press Sun 11 Oct 2026 14.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, are considering firing US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. A senior US official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s federal holiday. Trump donor accuses ‘grifter’ Kimberly Guilfoyle of $100,000 quid pro quo Read more The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled. In a series of stories, the Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill. Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the US embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her. After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.” But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm. “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on. The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied. A second US official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the state department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied. The second official could not say if a formal IG investigation had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. The state department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation. The top two Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House committee for oversight and government reform, Robert Garcia, Democrat of California, have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle. Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the US could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did. The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives. Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece. Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr. Explore more on these topics Trump administration US politics Donald Trump Marco Rubio US foreign policy news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.latintimes.com/nato-revealed.text: The Briefing: NATO's Supreme Allied Commander in Europe publicly revealed the alliance's "Theory of Victory" strategy for the first time at the Warsaw Security Forum, presenting the disclosure itself as a deliberate deterrence signal intended to convince Moscow that any attack on NATO territory would end in failure. An Associated Press tracker documents a stark increase in Russian hybrid attacks against Europe, from 59 recorded incidents in March 2025 to more than 200 at present, as Denmark's military intelligence service warns the campaign is likely to intensify in the months ahead. Norway has designated 2026 its year of "total defence," Sweden has rehearsed mass-casualty burial logistics as part of major NATO drills, and several European governments are restructuring civil preparedness — yet top officials emphasize that current intelligence does not indicate an imminent Russian attack on the alliance. The Warsaw Security Forum, which concluded Tuesday in the Polish capital after two days of high-level deliberations, brought into sharp focus what European security officials have quietly feared for months: the continent's entire defense architecture is being stress-tested in real time. At the center of proceedings stood General Alexus Grynkewich, the American four-star officer serving as NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, who used the gathering to release the alliance's so-called "Theory of Victory" — a strategic framework designed to make any Russian advance into NATO territory an unwinnable proposition before the first shot is ever fired.NATO's 'Theory of Victory' Goes PublicGrynkewich framed the public release of the strategy as a calculated deterrence act. By laying out precisely how NATO would respond to a Russian incursion, the alliance intends to persuade Moscow that the gamble carries an unacceptable cost. Advance reporting on the blueprint showed it draws heavily on lessons from the war in Ukraine, weaving drones and artificial intelligence into a layered framework that complements advantages NATO already holds in conventional airpower, including its fleet of F-35 fighter jets. At the Forum, asked whether the alliance could engage an adversary without delay, Grynkewich's answer was an unambiguous yes.The announcement landed against a charged backdrop. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, speaking at a press conference in Moscow on October 6, dismissed NATO's positioning and treated the new strategy as a subject for derision. He characterized Western alarm as cynical theater, while also warning that the escalating language of military preparation was itself reshaping the geopolitical landscape in dangerous ways — a cycle of rhetoric he cautioned could become self-sustaining.A Shadow War Already UnderwayNATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte reaffirmed this week that the alliance has solid action plans in place to address the surge in sabotage and drone incidents across Europe. Denmark's Defense Intelligence Service released a formal threat assessment simultaneously, warning that Russia is likely to escalate its hybrid campaign further — potentially through destructive cyberattacks that incapacitate critical infrastructure and sabotage operations that carry a real risk of casualties.An Associated Press interactive tracker monitoring hybrid incidents across Europe documented a sharp rise from 59 events in March 2025 to more than 200 at present. A NATO source noted the actual count could run considerably higher once cyberattacks are included, since alliance institutions absorb thousands of digital intrusions every month. Grynkewich has described Russia's escalating campaign — spanning airspace violations, arson, sabotage, and cyberattacks — as a deliberate effort to fracture Western collective resolve.Diplomatic Coordination at the Highest LevelRutte has worked in close alignment with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas to build a unified Western response — combining NATO's military deterrence posture with expanding economic sanctions against Moscow and an accelerating push for European defense industrial independence. Rutte has argued that the spike in hybrid incidents is itself evidence that Putin is losing in Ukraine, and that the most effective counter-response is sustained weapons support for Kyiv rather than escalatory alarm.Northern Europe Shifts Into a Higher GearPerhaps nowhere is the continental shift more tangible than across the Nordic countries. Norway formally designated 2026 its year of "total defence" — a concept mobilizing every sector of society, from the military to private businesses and individual households, to prepare for a major crisis or armed conflict. The country is working to reinstate a requirement that new large buildings include air raid shelters, an obligation that was lifted in 1998 following the Soviet Union's collapse. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre had already warned Norwegians in his New Year's address that war arriving on Norwegian soil was no longer unthinkable.Sweden took operational realism a step further. The country recently completed Aurora 26, a NATO exercise that mobilized roughly 18,000 troops from 13 nations and incorporated Ukrainian drone specialists as live training partners, giving alliance forces direct exposure to frontline counter-drone techniques developed in actual combat. Separately, the Church of Sweden — the country's statutory burial authority — has long operated under a civil defense planning directive requiring it to maintain burial capacity equivalent to five percent of the national population, a Cold War-era benchmark covering both military and civilian casualties nationwide.Separating Preparation From PanicCritical context is at risk of being lost in the online amplification of these developments. Fact-checking organizations across Europe, including Spain's RTVE, have identified as false viral social media posts claiming that the European Union issued a sudden emergency order requiring citizens to stockpile food ahead of an imminent war. The civilian preparedness guides circulating online were introduced gradually starting in late 2024 and into 2025 as part of longer-range deterrence planning — not as a reactive measure triggered by any approaching crisis.None of these preparations amount to an official forecast that a NATO-Russia war is imminent. Multiple senior officials — from Grynkewich to Rutte — have stated clearly that current intelligence does not point to an attack in the near term. The 2027 planning horizon, which Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk cited as a critical benchmark after meeting with Grynkewich, is treated in Warsaw and Brussels as a window to make deterrence so credible that conflict never materializes — not as a countdown to an inevitable confrontation.What sets this moment apart from previous cycles of European security anxiety is the institutional depth of the response. Governments are not simply issuing statements; they are reorganizing civil society, rebuilding shelters, restructuring defense budgets, and rehearsing catastrophic scenarios. Whether that commitment ultimately deters aggression or, as Lavrov suggested, inadvertently accelerates it remains an open and genuinely uncomfortable question.
